title: Signal Velocity: mini-OKRs & experiment journal
content:
Context:
Quick scratchpad for a 6-week micro-OKR sprint focused on personal signal velocity: moving small items end-to-end faster while preserving quality (less context-switch overhead, more deep work). Use this as my daily check-in + experiment log. Not for distribution — rough notes + raw numbers.

North-star (single line):
Increase 'meaningful throughput' from 4 -> 8 small deliverables/week (PRs, docs, experiments) while keeping context-switch time < 60 minutes/day.

Why this matters:
- I ship features slower than peers because of too many tiny interruptions and unclear prioritization rules.
- If I can reliably deliver more small, complete items, product and team momentum should improve.

Mini-OKRs (6-week cadence):
1) Throughput: 8 small ship items/week (baseline ~4). Definition: PR merged with tests + release notes or a documented experiment with owner review.
2) Focus blocks: 2 uninterrupted deep sessions/day (90+ minutes each) on at least 4 days/week.
3) Meeting debt: Reduce reactive meetings by 40% (tracking meeting invites accepted / declined).
4) Latency of decisions: Reduce time-to-review for my PRs to <24h for reviewers (by improving PR descriptions and pre-bake).

Measurement plan (daily signals):
- Completed items (count), PRs merged (count), doc/experiment completed (count) — tracked in a quick spreadsheet.
- Deep-work minutes (automatic log + calendar blocks).
- Number of ephemeral slack pings requiring immediate reply (self-tagged).
- Time spent on meetings (calendar total).

Hypotheses & Experiments (fast cycles):
H1: Batching notifications (check Slack 3x/day) will reduce context-switch time and increase completed items.
- Experiment: Mute non-essential channels, set Slack to 'batch mode' from 10:00-16:00, allow DMs for 'urgent' only. Start week 1.
- Metric: context-switch minutes/day (self-reported) and completed items/week.

H2: Pre-baked PR template + checklist reduces reviewer friction and shortens review time.
- Experiment: Use a checklist that includes 'what to test', 'approx perf impact', 'screenshots', and 'link to ticket'.
- Metric: time-to-merge, number of review cycles.

H3: Shorter meeting windows (25/50) and a weekly 'sync triage' reduce meetings and increase deep work minutes.
- Experiment: Block 25-minute core updates, batch async updates to a single triage doc.
- Metric: meeting minutes/week, deep-work minutes/day.

Daily log template (what I'll write each day):
- Date: YYYY-MM-DD
- Completed items: n (list)
- Deep sessions: count + minutes
- Interruptions: # + brief cause
- Wins / blockers
- Next day focus (top 3)

Sample entries (first two weeks — raw):
2026-01-20:
- Completed items: 2 (PR#1124: small routing fix; EXP: inbox batching config doc)
- Deep sessions: 1 (105 min)
- Interruptions: 6 (5 slack pings, 1 impromptu meeting)
- Wins: pre-baked PR checklist shortened review from 2 days -> 14 hours (Maya reviewed)
- Blockers: Calendar autopromote still allows some meeting invites to sneak in.
- Next day focus: finish refactor PR, schedule triage doc update

2026-01-22:
- Completed items: 4 (PR#1127: metrics tag; PR#1128: test cleanup; EXP: email batching rules; DOC: review notes)
- Deep sessions: 2 (90, 95 min)
- Interruptions: 2 (both DMs)
- Wins: hit 4 items in one day — felt 'flow' and fewer context switches
- Blockers: Need to formalize 'urgent DM' definition for the team
- Next day focus: prepare release notes, nudge reviewers

End-of-week retrospective (week 1):
- Outcome: Throughput = 10 items for the week (over target), deep-work average = 80 min/day, meetings down 33%.
- What worked: Slack batching reduced reactive replies; pre-baked PR checklist saved reviewer time.
- What didn't: Some teammates are confused by 'urgent-only' DM rule; calendar still has auto invites.
- Actionables: 1) Draft a 1-paragraph note about 'urgent DM' etiquette and post to channel; 2) Propose a calendar default decline policy to reduce auto-invites; 3) Share PR checklist as a small template in team repo.

Mid-sprint adjustments (week 3):
- Add a lightweight 'snooze-and-note' habit: when I see a non-urgent message, snooze for 2 hours and add a 1-line note in a 'respond-later' doc. This keeps the brain from jumping back.
- Try 2 x 90-minute blocks + 1 x 45-minute block on heavy-code days.

End-of-sprint retrospective (6 weeks):
- Final tallies (6-week aggregate): average throughput = 7.2 items/week (target 8), median time-to-review = 22 hours, deep-work median = 78 min/day, meetings down 41%.
- Key insights:
  - Notification batching gave the biggest single uplift to throughput.
  - Pre-baked PR checklist helped but only when reviewers read it; need to pair with a short cultural nudge (weekly highlight of good PRs that followed the checklist).
  - Blocking calendar as 'busy' discourages invites but aggressive org defaults still add meetings — need an org-level setting.
  - Personal slack: snooze-and-note reduced mental re-entry cost by ~30% per self-report.

Decisions going forward:
- Keep notification batching and snooze-and-note habit as baseline.
- Iterate PR template and add a 1-line 'review quick-check' in PR description to signal reviewers.
- Run a lightweight team sync to align on 'urgent' DM etiquette and announce calendar decline defaults.

Next sprint experiments:
- Micro-habit: first 45 min of day is 'no meetings' window for focused planning.
- Auto-review tags: try tagging 1 reviewer as 'first-pass' and 2nd reviewer as optional to speed merges.

Open questions / unresolved:
- How to measure 'quality of output' for small items? (customer impact vs. noise)
- Should I formalize the personal checklist into a small repo template or a shared Confluence page?

Notes-to-self:
- Keep logs minimal — I'm less likely to update if it feels onerous. 2–3 bullets/day is enough.
- Celebrate small wins publicly once every 2 weeks to build culture around quick shipping.

Links / references (quick):
- PR checklist template draft: github.com/redwood/repo/pulls/template-mini-PR
- Slack etiquette note: //channel/CC/productivity-experiments (draft in linked artifacts)
- Time tracking sheet: tinyurl.com/ava-miniokrs-2026

End of doc.
